Invective

in-VEK-tiv · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Invective is abusive or highly critical language.

The critic's review wasn't just negative -- it was pure invective, tearing apart every choice the director had made.

Worked Example

The coach's halftime speech was less a strategy talk than a stream of invective, hurling insults at every player who had missed a shot.

Invective is abusive, insulting language -- the coach isn't offering constructive criticism, just harsh verbal attacks.

How Invective Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

abuse

abuse: harsh, insulting language

vituperation

vituperation: bitter, abusive language directed at someone

Antonyms

praise

praise: words expressing approval

compliment

compliment: a polite expression of admiration

How Strong Is It? — criticism → invective → tongue-lashing

criticism vs. invective

criticism vs. invective: Criticism is negative feedback, but it isn't necessarily abusive or insulting.

tongue-lashing vs. invective

tongue-lashing vs. invective: A tongue-lashing is a furious, sustained verbal attack -- an even more intense burst of invective.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: against, into (Latin)

root — vect

root — vect: carried (Latin vehere, 'to carry')

suffix — -ive

suffix — -ive: tending to, having the nature of (Latin -ivus)

Put it together

Put it together: Invective comes from Latin in- ('against') + vehere ('to carry') + -ivus -- literally 'carried against' someone, meaning language hurled at them as an attack.

Root Check

Word Choice

Invective is the abusive language itself -- the harsh words someone actually says or writes -- which makes it different from rancor (the underlying bitter feeling) and vilify (the act of using such language to damage someone's reputation).
